analysis.summary: Kubernetes v1.37 是一个功能丰富的版本，核心价值在于引入了声明式的 Pod 驱逐 API、显著提升了 DRA（动态资源分配）功能的成熟度与性能，并修复了多个关键的安全与稳定性问题。
key_changes: 引入声明式 EvictionRequest API，支持优雅驱逐 Pod - [PR #137050](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137050) - **影响：** 为自动化运维提供了新的 API 原语，可替代部分 `kubectl drain` 的使用场景。
DRA 调度器性能优化：为 ResourceClaim 事件添加 PreQueueingHint 扩展点，将 O(N) 的 Pod 重评估优化为 O(1) - [PR #138916](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138916) - **影响：** 大幅提升大规模集群中使用 DRA 时的调度器响应速度。
kube-proxy nftables 模式默认启用 netlink 支持以提升性能 - [PR #137536](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137536) - **影响：** 减少规则同步时的命令执行开销，提升网络代理性能。
支持内存卷（如 tmpfs）的动态在线扩容 - [PR #139425](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139425) - **影响：** 允许在不重启 Pod 的情况下调整内存卷大小，提升应用灵活性。
KubeletInUserNamespace 功能升级至 Beta - [PR #134639](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134639) - **影响：** 改善在用户命名空间（如 rootless 模式）下运行 Kubelet 的支持。
HostnameOverride 功能门控升级至 GA - [PR #139116](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139116) - **影响：** 功能稳定，可安全用于覆盖节点主机名。
important_bugfixes: 修复 DRA 设备分配重试时可能导致设备列表重复的 bug - [PR #140274](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140274) - **影响：** 防止容器启动失败或设备被重复挂载。
修复 cgroup v2 下 Pod 级别 CPU 请求状态读取错误的问题 - [PR #137660](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/137660) - **影响：** 确保资源监控和报告的数据准确性。
修复 In-Place Pod 垂直伸缩时，MemoryQoS 保护可能丢失的问题 - [PR #140262](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140262) - **影响：** 保障 Pod 内存服务质量在资源调整期间不受影响。
修复旧版本客户端通过 `pods/status` 更新时可能误清空 DRA 状态字段，导致 Pod 卡在 Terminating 的问题 - [PR #139876](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139876) - **影响：** 解决与旧客户端（如某些 CNI 插件）交互时的 Pod 终止阻塞问题。
修复 kubelet 重启后，Pod 初始化检测逻辑可能导致 init 容器未正确重启的问题 - [PR #138514](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138514) - **影响：** 提升节点重启后 Pod 恢复的可靠性。
security_issues: 放宽对包含 `CAP_SYSADMIN` 能力但 `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` 的 Pod 的验证 - [PR #138834](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138834) - **风险级别：** 中 - **影响：** 此变更修复了之前过于严格的验证（Issue #119568），允许了原本被错误拒绝的安全配置。但需重新评估集群安全策略，确保此变更符合预期。

识别 `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` 无法完全防止通过危险能力（如 CAP_NET_ADMIN）进行权限提升的问题 - [Issue #131336](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/131336) - **风险级别：** 中 - **影响：** 这是一个已知限制，用户需意识到仅设置 `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` 不足以防御所有权限提升途径，应结合其他安全措施。
performance_improvements: 调度器为仅使用 `kubernetes.io/hostname` 拓扑的 Pod 间亲和性/反亲和性规则启用快速评估路径 - [PR #138198](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138198) - **提升：** 将 O(N*M) 的集群范围扫描优化为仅检查当前节点，显著降低调度延迟。
kube-proxy nftables 模式优化，为单端点 Service 避免使用 numgen map，减少规则集映射数量以提升同步速度 - [PR #140723](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140723) - **提升：** 缓解 Service 数量增长时同步时间超线性增长的问题（Issue #139513）。
API Server 默认启用 `ConcurrentWatchObjectDecode` 特性门控（Beta），支持并行解码 Watch 事件 - [PR #139679](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139679) - **提升：** Watch 缓存初始化性能提升约 45%。
为 nftables 模式的本地主机 NodePorts 提供支持 - [PR #138427](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/138427) - **提升：** 改善了本地开发测试和本地镜像仓库等场景的体验。
breaking_changes: client-go 完成 Context 支持，移除了绝大多数 `context.TODO()` 调用，引入了新的上下文感知 API - [PR #129125](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129125) - **影响：** 直接使用底层 client-go 库的代码可能需要适配新的 API 签名以传递 Context。
`PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` 特性门控在 Beta 阶段默认被禁用 - [PR #140081](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/140081) - **影响：** 依赖此功能获取容器统计信息的用户需要显式启用该门控。
`DRAPrioritizedList` 特性门控（已在 1.36 GA）被锁定为默认启用且不可禁用 - [PR #139110](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/139110) - **影响：** 升级后无法再关闭此功能。
recommendations: **升级前必须测试：** 由于包含大量 API 变更和 DRA 相关改动，请在非生产环境充分测试工作负载的兼容性与稳定性，特别是使用了 DRA、Pod 垂直伸缩或自定义调度器插件的集群。
**评估安全策略：** 仔细审查 PR #138834 关于 `CAP_SYSADMIN` 验证的变更，确认其是否会影响您现有的 Pod 安全策略或合规要求。
**检查客户端兼容性：** 如果集群中运行着使用旧版 client-go（早于引入 DRA 字段版本）的控制器或插件（如某些 CNI），升级前请参考 PR #139876 评估 Pod 终止风险，并考虑更新这些组件。
**关注性能监控：** 升级后，密切关注调度器（特别是 DRA 相关）、kube-proxy（nftables 模式）和 API Server 的性能指标，验证性能改进效果并发现潜在问题。
**利用新功能：** 计划使用新的 EvictionRequest API 来优化节点维护等自动化流程，替代传统的 `kubectl drain` 命令调用。
analysis.risk_assessment: 整体风险评估：**中等**。此版本引入了重要的新 API 和大量优化，但同时也包含对核心组件（kubelet、调度器、kube-proxy）的深度修改。DRA 功能快速演进，相关修复较多，表明该区域仍处于活跃状态。建议的升级时机是在 v1.37 稳定版发布后，经过至少 2-4 周的测试环境验证。需要特别关注的方面包括：DRA 设备管理的正确性、Pod 终止流程、调度器性能变化，以及任何依赖 client-go 上下文的自定义控制器/工具的兼容性。

129125.title: client-go: finish context support
129125.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The main purpose is to replace context.TODO with a context provided by the caller. A secondary purpose is to enable contextual logging.

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129109 for an introduction of the approach taken most of the time when adding alternative context-aware APIs. See commit messages for additional information.

Most likely this will be merged by creating smaller PRs.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
client-go: with very few exceptions, context.TODO calls got removed by introducing new APIs where the caller passes in the context. Log calls use the logger provided by the caller when available.
```

134037.title: KEP-3926: implement dry-run support for unsafe corrupt object deletion
134037.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR implements dry-run support for the unsafe corrupt object deletion feature introduced in KEP-3926.

This enhancement allows administrators to safely test corrupt object deletion operations before executing them, providing an important safety mechanism for this potentially cluster-breaking operation.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
 
Fixes #

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This builds upon the existing unsafe deletion functionality from #127513. The dry-run implementation follows Kubernetes' standard dry-run patterns and maintains backward compatibility.

Key changes:

- Removed validation restriction in that blocked dry-run with unsafe deletion options
- Enhanced `corrupt_obj_deleter.go` to handle dry-run requests appropriately
- Added comprehensive test coverage for dry-run scenarios in integration tests

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

This feature is feature-gated by `AllowUnsafeMalformedObjectDeletion`:

```release-note
The unsafe corrupt object deletion feature now supports dry-run mode, allowing administrators to test deletion operations safely before execution.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:

- KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3927

138916.title: scheduler: add PreQueueingHint extension point to narrow pod evaluation on events
138916.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

   /kind feature
   /sig scheduling

   #### What this PR does / why we need it:

   Adds a `PreQueueingHintFn` extension point to the scheduling framework, called once per event to return a set of pod keys to evaluate instead of scanning all unschedulable pods. This addresses the O(N) requeue bottleneck identified in #138095 using the extension-point approach agreed upon in #138531.

   The DRA plugin implements `PreQueueingHintFn` for ResourceClaim events: for ResourceClaimTemplate-based claims (per-pod claims with a Pod OwnerReference), it returns only the owning pod's key, reducing the requeue path from O(N) to O(1). For shared claims or non-templated claims without a single pod owner, it returns nil to fall back to evaluating all pods
   (existing behavior).

   Additionally, ResourceClaim event handling is decoupled from the informer thread using an async workqueue, preventing the informer from blocking on scheduling queue lock acquisition during claim events.

   Both optimizations are gated behind the `SchedulerPreQueueingHints` feature gate (alpha, default=false).

   #### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

   Fixes #138095
   Supersedes #138531

   #### Special notes for your reviewer:

   This implements the extension-point approach recommended by @pohly, @mm4tt, and @macsko in #138531 — plugin-specific logic stays in the plugin, the framework provides a generic `PreQueueingHintFn` that any plugin can implement.

   AI tools (Kiro CLI) were used to assist with development and testing of this change.


   #### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
No


```release-note
Added a new beta feature gate SchedulerPreQueueingHints (on by default). When enabled, scheduler plugins can provide a PreQueueingHintFn that narrows the set of pods evaluated on cluster events, improving scheduling throughput. The DRA plugin implements this to optimize ResourceClaimTemplate-based workloads.
```

139921.title: kubelet: populate Node UID on recorded node events (best-effort)
139921.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The kubelet builds one static node `ObjectReference` at startup with only kind and name, no UID, because the reference must work before the Node exists in the apiserver (#42701). As a result every node event the kubelet records has `involvedObject.uid` unset, so consumers that match by UID (for example `kubectl describe node`) silently drop them.

This PR keeps that behavior but adds a `nodeRefWithUID()` helper that returns a per-call copy of the reference with the UID filled in from the node lister cache (no apiserver round-trip). When the UID isn't known yet, such as early startup or standalone mode, it falls back to the name-only reference. Copying per call keeps the shared reference immutable and the helper safe under concurrent event recording.

The kubelet's own node event sites now use it: `recordNodeStatusEvent`, `recordEvent`, and the `ContainerGCFailed`, `ImageGCFailed`, `KubeletSetupFailed`, `StartingKubelet`, and `CgroupV1` events. This covers the node-status events users most commonly inspect.

A few node events are out of scope. Events emitted before the node is registered genuinely can't carry a UID. Several subsystems also capture the static reference by pointer and emit their own node events: the oom watcher, eviction manager, image GC manager, node-shutdown manager, and DNS configurer. Routing those through a UID-aware reference needs a getter threaded into each subsystem, so it's left as follow-up. #138362 remains the complementary CLI-side fix.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Related to #138524

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

The shared reference is used by pointer across subsystems, so the helper copies rather than mutates it to avoid a data race. The added unit test runs under `-race` and asserts the shared `nodeRef` is never mutated.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
kubelet: node events recorded by the kubelet now populate `involvedObject.uid` on a best-effort basis once the node is registered, so node events can be correlated by UID (for example in `kubectl describe node`). The UID is resolved once and not refreshed afterward. If a node is deleted and recreated with a new UID while the kubelet keeps running, its events continue to use the original UID until the kubelet restarts.
```

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`PrepareResources` appends devices to a claim's `DriverState` as each per-driver `NodePrepareResources` response comes in. 140437.title: DRA: skip the counter check for a persisted shared device
140437.body:
## What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

## What this PR does / why we need it

The structured allocator double-counts a shared counter for a persisted allow-multiple device that is recorded only by share ID.

When a device both allows multiple allocations (`DRAConsumableCapacity`) and consumes shared counters (`DRAPartitionableDevices`), a persisted shared allocation whose result carries a `ShareID` but no `ConsumedCapacity` is represented in `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs` with no entry in `AggregatedCapacity`. Counter availability is initialized through `IsDeviceAllocated`, which recognizes `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`, so the persisted allocation already subtracts the device's counters from the pool. But `deviceCapacityInUse`, which drives the counter-check skip for allow-multiple devices, looks only at `AggregatedCapacity`. It misses the persisted share, the counter check runs again, and a second claim sharing the device is rejected with a false "Insufficient counters".

This makes `deviceCapacityInUse` recognize `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`, the same way `IsDeviceAllocated` already does, in both the incubating and experimental allocators. The stable allocator does not support `ConsumableCapacity` and is unaffected.

## Which issue(s) this PR fixes

Fixes #140433

## Special notes for your reviewer

The check scans `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs` per candidate, matching the existing `IsDeviceAllocated` pattern, rather than precomputing a `Set[DeviceID]`. This keeps a single source of truth, with no second copy of the persisted shared state, at the cost of an O(n) scan gated behind `allowMultipleAllocations`. A derived index can be added later if the scan shows up in profiles.

Regression coverage in the shared `allocatortesting` table:
- `partitionable-consumable-capacity-shared-device-counter-not-recharged`: the issue's case. It fails on the unfixed allocator with "Insufficient counters" and passes with the fix, in both the incubating and experimental allocators.
## Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Fixed a DRA consumable-capacity scheduling bug: a device that consumes shared counters could have them counted twice when it already had a persisted shared allocation with no consumed capacity, wrongly rejecting a later claim for the same device and leaving the pod pending.
```

140442.title: DRA: reject an out-of-range consumable-capacity request
140442.body:
**What type of PR is this?**

/kind bug
/sig node
/wg device-management

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

`roundUpRange` rounds a consumable-capacity request up to a Step multiple using `Quantity.Value()` int64 arithmetic. A request near `MaxInt64` makes `min + step*n` wrap to a negative value that sits below the request and passes the capacity check, and a request above `MaxInt64` wraps in `Value()` itself and reads as a satisfiable-looking value. On the fractional path the request can pass the milli-value range in the same way. The value cannot then be rounded or compared reliably.

Today the request comes from the ResourceSlice, so in practice it is well-formed. Shared consumable capacity (#140084) takes the request from the user's ResourceClaim, so an out-of-range request becomes user-reachable, and skipping the device to try the next one would let such a request drive the scheduler into backtracking.

`roundUpRange` and its helpers now return `(Quantity, error)`. A request, or a rounded value, that cannot be represented (past `MaxInt64` on the integer path, or past the milli-value range on the fractional path) returns `errCapacityRequestNotRepresentable`, and the allocator aborts the allocation with that error instead of skipping the device. A request for a capacity the device does not define still skips, since another device may define it. The int64 and milli fast paths are unchanged for representable inputs. Both allocators are covered by allocatortesting cases and the per-allocator unit tables.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:

Fixes #140441

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

- For a device that defines all the requested capacity names, representability is resolved for every capacity before the policy and capacity checks, so a request that overflows aborts regardless of Go's map iteration order, rather than being masked by another capacity the map happens to visit first. A request naming a capacity the device does not define is a separate, earlier skip, since another device may define it.
- Aborting on the first device whose arithmetic overflows is fail-closed: a later device that could satisfy the request by exact comparison is not tried. That is what removes the backtracking, and an allocatortesting case pins it. A unit test pins the fatal-over-soft ordering within a device.
- The allocator rejects a resolved capacity that is negative before recording it: a stored ResourceSlice or ResourceClaim from before stricter validation could carry one, and admission does not re-check existing objects, so relying on admission alone is not enough. Overflow stays the allocator's job because it depends on the device's int64-versus-milli math that admission cannot see. Broader magnitude validation of a user-facing request belongs in #140084, and a malformed RequestPolicy is tracked in #140472.
- Split out of the #140161 review at @pohly's suggestion, as the non-fractional `Value()` path. @sunya-ch handled the fractional milli-value path in #140161 and left a `TODO (#140441)` that this PR resolves.
- #140161 has merged; this PR is rebased onto it.

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**

```release-note
Fixed capacity accounting in the DRA consumable-capacity allocator. A capacity request that a device's integer or milli-value range arithmetic cannot represent, or that resolves to a negative value, is now rejected instead of being treated as satisfiable and wrongly allocating a device or capping it to a smaller value.
```

140661.title: admission/namespace/lifecycle: allow updates to resources in deleted namespaces
140661.body:
## Problem

The NamespaceLifecycle admission plugin rejects both Create and Update requests when the target namespace has been fully deleted from storage. While blocking Creates is correct (no new content should appear in a deleted namespace), blocking Updates prevents controllers from re-writing objects that still exist in etcd.

This causes a bug in the storage version migrator (#140655): when orphaned objects remain in etcd after their namespace is deleted, the migrator's Patch is rejected with NotFound by NamespaceLifecycle. The migrator treats NotFound as "object deleted, safe to skip" and reports migration as complete, even though the object was never re-written.

## Fix

Allow Update operations through early, alongside Delete, which is already allowed regardless of namespace state (line 101). The storage layer validates object existence and will reject the Update if the object itself is gone.

Only Create operations now proceed to the namespace existence check. Patches that would create new objects are classified as Create operations by the admission layer and remain blocked.

## Note on admission webhooks

Admission webhooks that match Update operations will now receive requests for objects in deleted namespaces. This is consistent with Delete operations, which already bypass the namespace existence check. Webhooks that look up the namespace should already handle the missing-namespace case gracefully, since they must do so for Deletes.

## Test

- Updated `TestAdmissionNamespaceDoesNotExist`: Update assertion flipped from "expect error" to "expect allowed"
- New `TestAdmissionNamespaceFullyDeleted`: verifies Create is rejected, Update is allowed, and Delete is allowed when the namespace is fully deleted (live lookup returns NotFound)
- Mutation tested: reverting the fix causes both Update assertions to fail

## Context

Per discussion in #140655, @liggitt suggested fixing this at the admission layer rather than in the migrator. This PR implements his option 2: allow the update of the orphaned object if the object still exists.

/sig api-machinery
/kind bug

```release-note
Fixes handling of admission to allow updates to namespaced objects that exist after their namespace was deleted.
```

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`EventedPLEG` previously acted as an alternative PLEG implementation. When enabled, it wrote pod status to the kubelet cache and emitted `PodLifecycleEvent`s directly, while `GenericPLEG` ran with a much longer relist period and served as a fallback.

That design gave two components responsibility for publishing runtime state and introduced cache ownership, timestamp ordering, and `SyncPod` consistency concerns.

GenericPLEG now supports on-demand per-pod relisting through #137362. When `SyncPod` performs one or more runtime operations and completes without an aggregate error, it schedules a post-sync relist for that pod. Kubelet-driven runtime transitions therefore no longer require a second PLEG implementation to publish status.

This PR changes the architecture as follows:

- `GenericPLEG` always runs at its normal relist period and remains the sole PLEG implementation.
- `GenericPLEG` is the only component that relists authoritative runtime state, updates the pod cache, and emits `PodLifecycleEvent`s.
- `EventedPLEG` no longer implements `PodLifecycleEventGenerator`, accesses the pod cache, emits lifecycle events, or participates in PLEG health checks.
- `EventedPLEG` is reduced to an optional CRI event watcher whose only dependency on GenericPLEG is `RequestRelist`.
- The watcher uses selected CRI container termination events as low-latency hints for crash-like transitions that may occur independently of `SyncPod`.
- `EventedPLEG` now declares a feature dependency on `PLEGOnDemandRelist`, preventing configurations where the watcher is enabled but its relist requests are disabled.

139604.body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Adds Prometheus metrics for topology-aware scheduling (TAS) pod group placement, so the volume and latency of the placement evaluation phase can be observed.

3 alpha metrics are introduced, gated on the beta `TopologyAwareWorkloadScheduling` feature gate by default off (since they are only registered when TAS is enabled). Metrics are defined in [KEP-5732](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/5732):

- `scheduler_generated_placements_total` counter of candidate placements generated when scheduling pod groups.
- `scheduler_placement_evaluations_total` counter of candidate placements evaluated when scheduling pod groups, split by `feasible`/`infeasible` result.
- `scheduler_placement_evaluation_duration_seconds` latency of evaluating a single candidate placement, split by `feasible`/`infeasible` result.

The TAS pod group placement algorithm phases:
1. generation: generate candidate placements 
2. evaluation: per placement loop try to fit each candidate
3. scoring: pick the best among feasible placements (only if there are more than 1 feasible placement)

The placement generation and scoring phases are intentionally not given dedicated metrics, since they are already covered by `scheduler_framework_extension_point_duration_seconds` with the [`PlacementGenerate`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L2076) and [`PlacementScore`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/framework.go#L1493) extension points. 
There is also existing `podgroup_scheduling_algorithm_duration_seconds` which measures the overall pod group scheduling cycle, so this PR focuses on the per-placement evaluation.

139876.title: apiserver/pod: preserve DRA status fields when old clients clear them via pods/status
139876.body:
## What this PR does / why we need it

When a client that predates the DRA fields (`ResourceClaimStatuses`,
`ExtendedResourceClaimStatus`, `NodeAllocatableResourceClaimStatuses`)
issues a `pods/status` update, those fields are absent from the Pod it
sends back. The apiserver stores the update as-is, effectively clearing
DRA status. On the next termination sync, kubelet has no claim info from
the pod status and logs:

```
unprepare dynamic resources: pod "…": ResourceClaim not created yet
```

This leaves pods permanently stuck in `Terminating`.

**Root cause** (from #139772 discussion): Multus CNI uses
`network-attachment-definition-client` which pins `k8s.io/client-go
v0.29.0` — predating DRA fields. It calls `UpdateStatus` to write an
annotation, but the round-tripped Pod has the DRA fields zeroed.

**Fix**: extend `podStatusStrategy.PrepareForUpdate` to restore all three
DRA-related status fields from the old pod when the incoming update omits
them. This applies to running and terminating pods because the old client
can issue status updates throughout the pod lifecycle. For the two slice
fields, an explicit non-nil empty slice (`[]`) remains an allowed way to
clear the field.

The scheduler's Unreserve path now sends that explicit empty list when it
clears `NodeAllocatableResourceClaimStatuses`; its previous generic status
patch serialized the clear as an omitted field.

`DropDisabledPodFields` runs afterwards and will still strip the fields
when the corresponding feature gate is disabled, so there is no
interaction with the feature gate lifecycle.

This complements the kubelet-side resilience fix in #139845.

## Which issue(s) this PR is related to

Fixes #139772

## Type of change

/kind feature
/sig node
/sig api-machinery
/wg device-management
/triage accepted

## Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
Data in DRA-related fields in pod status (resourceClaimStatuses, extendedResourceClaimStatus, and nodeAllocatableResourceClaimStatuses) is now preserved when handling pod status updates that omit those fields. This prevents data loss due to updates from old clients accidentally unsetting these DRA fields, which could leave pods permanently stuck in Terminating.
```

## Testing

- Added eight cases to `TestStatusPrepareForUpdate` covering omitted DRA
  fields on running and terminating pods, plus explicit empty-slice updates.
- Added `TestDRAStatusPreservedOnStatusUpdate`, which exercises the
  running-pod regression and explicit empty-list clearing through the
  apiserver.
- Updated the scheduler Unreserve test to assert the explicit empty-list
  merge patch used to clear `NodeAllocatableResourceClaimStatuses`.
- `make test WHAT=./pkg/registry/core/pod GOFLAGS=-v`
- `make test WHAT=./pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/dynamicresources GOFLAGS=-v`
- `make test-integration WHAT=./test/integration/pods GOFLAGS=-v KUBE_TEST_ARGS='-run ^TestDRAStatusPreservedOnStatusUpdate$'`

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds two labels, `trigger` and `outcome`, to the existing ALPHA metric `route_controller_route_sync_total`, so operators can see not just how many route reconciles run, but why they ran and whether they actually changed anything.

- `trigger` distinguishes reconciles caused by an observed node change (`node_change`) from those caused by the informer's periodic resync (`periodic`). Per KEP 5237, the route controller uses the resync (events where the old and new Node are identical) as a signal to run its regular cleanup reconcile.
- `outcome` records whether the reconcile created or deleted at least one route (`changed`) or was a no-op (`noop`).

Previously the metric only counted total reconciles, with no way to tell periodic cleanup passes from node-change-driven ones, or whether those periodic passes were just no-ops or routinely fixing drift. The new labels give operators visibility into how often periodic reconciliation is actually correcting route drift.

119568.title: Incorrect validation of `allowPrivilegeEscalation` with `SYS_ADMIN` capability
119568.body:
### What happened?

Validation logic to disallow `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` in combination with `SYS_ADMIN` capability checks for `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` instead of `SYS_ADMIN` (see [security context validation](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d17f3ba/pkg/apis/core/validation/validation.go#L6823)).

Adding `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` to the security context does not add the `cap_sys_admin` capability to the container, while the `SYS_ADMIN` capability does add it.

⚠️ Tested with containerd, CRI-O seems to "correctly" add the capability when using `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`.

### What did you expect to happen?

A container that has a `securityContext` set, with both `allowPrivilegedEscalation` set to `false` and configuration to receive `cap_sys_admin` privileges, should be rejected.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Following pod logs the current capabilities of the container and then exits.

example pod, that is rejected:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine
    command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add -U libcap && capsh --print']
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop:
        - "ALL"
        add:
        - "CAP_SYS_ADMIN"
```

example pod, that is scheduled with `cap_sys_admin` capability and `allowPrivilegeEscalation`:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test
spec:
  containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine
    command: ['sh', '-c', 'apk add -U libcap && capsh --print']
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop:
        - "ALL"
        add:
        - "SYS_ADMIN"
```
> Current: cap_sys_admin=ep

### Anything else we need to know?

This is a small fix for a single incorrect validation, but the problem is that it's possible to create containers that do not receive the expected capabilities without receiving a warning (see [related discussion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117812#discussion_r1238776853)).

There is a warning, that "...you must omit the `CAP_` portion of the constant..." in the how to [set capabilities for a container](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/#set-capabilities-for-a-container) documentation, but none of that is validated.

131336.title: allowPrivilegeEscalation:false insufficient for privilege escalation prevention
131336.body:
The issue relates to how allowPrivilegeEscalation: false doesn't prevent all forms of privilege escalation through dangerous capabilities. 

When a container's security context sets allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, the current validation only blocks CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability. However, other dangerous capabilities that can also lead to privilege escalation are still allowed.

Technical Details:
1. Current Validation:
   - Blocks: CAP_SYS_ADMIN when allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
   - Allows: CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_MODULE, CAP_SYS_PTRACE, etc.

2. Example:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: busybox
    image: busybox
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        add: ["CAP_NET_ADMIN", "CAP_SYS_MODULE"]  # This is allowed but can lead to privilege escalation
```

3. Dangerous Capabilities Still Allowed:
   - CAP_NET_ADMIN: Network stack manipulation, potential for network namespace escape
   - CAP_SYS_MODULE: Loading kernel modules
   - CAP_SYS_PTRACE: Process debugging and memory access
   - CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH: Bypass file permission checks
   - CAP_SYS_RAWIO: Direct I/O access
   - CAP_AUDIT_CONTROL: Audit system manipulation

Impact:
- False sense of security when using allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
- Privilege escalation still possible through allowed capabilities

Proposed Fix:
Extend the validation to block all dangerous capabilities when allowPrivilegeEscalation is set to false.

I’d love to hear your thoughts! Have you run into situations where `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` didn’t cut it? 
Thanks

138095.title: DRA: scheduler performance issue with ResourceClaim event handling
138095.body:
## Problem

When a ResourceClaim is created or updated, the scheduler's event handler calls `MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue`, which iterates **every pod** in the unschedulable queue under an exclusive lock to determine which pods should be requeued. At scale, this becomes a  bottleneck.

On a 10,000-node KWOK cluster scheduling DRA pods, `MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue` and its callees consume **~9% of total scheduler CPU** in a 30-second profile window:

```
                                          cum   cum%
  MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue          9.24%
    moveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue        9.15%
      movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue     9.05%
        isPodWorthRequeuing              6.82%
```

The call chain is:

```
informer callback (ResourceClaim Add/Update)
  → MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue()     // acquires exclusive lock
    → moveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue()   // iterates ALL unschedulable pods
      → movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue()
        → isPodWorthRequeuing()         // per-pod hint evaluation
```

Every ResourceClaim event triggers a full scan of the unschedulable pod pool. With N pending pods and M claim events, this is O(N×M) work under the scheduling queue lock, blocking `Pop()` and all other queue operations.

### Observation

ResourceClaims created from a `ResourceClaimTemplate` have an `OwnerReference` pointing to the pod that triggered their creation. For these per-pod claims, only the owning pod needs to be requeued — not every pod in the unschedulable pool.

### Profiling environment

- Kubernetes v1.34.5 (stock scheduler, no modifications)
- 10,000 KWOK nodes, each with one ResourceSlice (1 device per pool)
- DRA pods each with one per-pod ResourceClaim (AllocationMode=All)
- 30-second CPU profile captured during active scheduling

Opening this issue to start the discussion and explore a fix. One possible
approach is to leverage the pod OwnerReference on per-pod claims to requeue
only the affected pod instead of scanning the entire unschedulable pool.

140433.title: DRA structured allocator double-counts a shared counter for a persisted allow-multiple device recorded only by share ID
140433.body:
### What happened?

When a device both allows multiple allocations (`DRAConsumableCapacity`) and consumes shared counters (`DRAPartitionableDevices`), a persisted shared allocation can cause the device's counters to be accounted for twice during a later scheduling cycle.

This occurs when the earlier allocation result contains a `ShareID` but no `ConsumedCapacity`. In that state, the device is represented in `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`, but it has no entry in `AggregatedCapacity`.

When a later claim attempts to share the same device, the structured allocator rejects it with:

```text
Insufficient counters device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
Device not usable device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
```

The persisted allocation has already caused the device's counters to be subtracted from the pool. The new allocation attempt nevertheless charges the same counters again, causing a false counter exhaustion.

### Root cause

`allocateDevice` skips the counter availability check for an allow-multiple device only when `deviceCapacityInUse` returns true:

```go
skipCounterCheck := allowMultipleAllocations && alloc.deviceCapacityInUse(device.id)
```

`deviceCapacityInUse` only checks persisted aggregated capacity and capacity reserved during the current allocation search:

```go
func (alloc *allocator) deviceCapacityInUse(deviceID DeviceID) bool {
    _, found := alloc.allocatedState.AggregatedCapacity[deviceID]
    return found || alloc.allocatingCapacityForAnyClaim(deviceID)
}
```

A persisted shared allocation without consumed capacity has:

```text
AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs: contains device1/share-A
AggregatedCapacity:       no entry for device1
```

Counter availability is initialized through `IsDeviceAllocated`, which does recognize `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`. Therefore, the persisted allocation already causes device1's counters to be subtracted from the available pool.

However, `deviceCapacityInUse` does not recognize `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`. Consequently:

```text
persisted share ID
    ↓
IsDeviceAllocated(device1) == true
    ↓
device1's counters are subtracted from availableCounters
    ↓
deviceCapacityInUse(device1) == false
    ↓
skipCounterCheck == false
    ↓
checkAvailableCounters charges device1's counters again
    ↓
false "Insufficient counters"
```

This appears to be a remaining edge case after #134103. That change added the counter-check skip when some device capacity is already in use, but a shared allocation without a persisted `AggregatedCapacity` entry is not covered by that predicate.

### What did you expect to happen?

The existing allocation already represents device1 as a shared, allow-multiple device, and its shared counters have already been accounted for.

Because the device permits multiple allocations and the new allocation consumes no per-share capacity, a second claim should be able to share device1 without charging its physical shared counters again.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The following case can be added to the shared `allocatortesting` table:

```go
"partitionable-consumable-capacity-shared-device-counter-not-recharged": {
    features: Features{
        PartitionableDevices: true,
        ConsumableCapacity:   true,
    },
    // device1 already has a persisted shared allocation. It is represented
    // only by a share ID, with no AggregatedCapacity entry.
    allocatedSharedDeviceIDs: sets.New(
        internal.MakeSharedDeviceID(
            MakeDeviceID(driverA, pool1, device1),
            &fixedShareID,
        ),
    ),
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claimWithRequests(claim0, nil, request(req0, classA, 1)),
    ),
    classes: objects(class(classA, driverA)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
        sliceWithDevices(
            slice1,
            node1,
            resourcePool(pool1, 2),
            driverA,
            device(device1, nil, nil).
                withAllowMultipleAllocations().
                withDeviceCounterConsumption(
                    deviceCounterConsumption(
                        counterSet1,
                        map[string]resource.Quantity{
                            "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                        },
                    ),
                ),
        ),
        sliceWithCounterSets(
            slice2,
            node1,
            resourcePool(pool1, 2),
            driverA,
            counterSet(
                counterSet1,
                map[string]resource.Quantity{
                    "c": resource.MustParse("1"),
                },
            ),
        ),
    ),
    node: node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{
        allocationResult(
            localNodeSelector(node1),
            deviceRequestAllocationResult(
                req0,
                driverA,
                pool1,
                device1,
            ).withConsumedCapacity(&fixedShareID, nil),
        ),
    },
},
```

The shared test harness replaces generated share IDs with `fixedShareID` before comparing results. The expected `fixedShareID` above therefore does not imply that the new allocation reuses the persisted allocation's actual share ID.

On commit `16e45f3b5e6a76a1ac741550e3a65980eea783c2`, this case fails with no allocation result and logs:

```text
Insufficient counters device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
Device not usable device="driver-a/pool-1/device-1"
```

It passes when the counter-check skip also recognizes that device1 already has a persisted shared allocation.

The failure is reproduced in the incubating allocator, which is selected for this feature combination, and in the experimental allocator, which carries the same predicate. The stable allocator does not support `ConsumableCapacity` and is not affected.

### Anything else we need to know?

The skip predicate needs to recognize a persisted shared allocation represented by `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs`, even when the device has no entry in `AggregatedCapacity`.

A narrow fix could add a lookup for the underlying `DeviceID` in the persisted shared-device state while retaining the existing `deviceCapacityInUse` behavior for allocations with consumed capacity and allocations created during the current search.

Because this check runs in the allocator's per-candidate search path, it may be preferable to precompute a `Set[DeviceID]` from `AllocatedSharedDeviceIDs` when constructing the allocator rather than scanning every shared ID for each candidate.

140441.title: DRA: consumable-capacity roundUpRange overflows int64 for a large capacity request, allocating a device it cannot satisfy
140441.body:
### What happened?

The structured DRA allocator's consumable-capacity rounding overflows int64 for a large capacity request, so a device is allocated for a request it cannot satisfy and its consumed capacity is recorded as a negative value.

`roundUpRange` (in `structured/internal/{incubating,experimental}/consumable_capacity.go`) rounds a request up to the next `Min + n*Step` using int64 arithmetic:

```go
requestedInt64 := requestedVal.Value()
step := validRange.Step.Value()
min := validRange.Min.Value()
added := (requestedInt64 - min)
n := added / step
mod := added % step
if mod != 0 {
    n += 1
}
val := min + step*n
return *resource.NewQuantity(val, resource.BinarySI)
```

For a request near `math.MaxInt64` with a `ValidRange` that has a `Step`, `min + step*n` exceeds `math.MaxInt64` and wraps to a negative value. That negative consumed capacity then passes both the policy check (`violateValidRange`: a negative value is below `Max`) and the over-capacity check (`clone[name].Cmp(cap.Value)`: a negative value is below the device capacity), so the device is accepted.

#### Impact

- A request far larger than the device's capacity is accepted instead of rejected.
- The device's consumed capacity for that allocation is recorded as a large negative quantity, which corrupts the running total for that shared allow-multiple device, so later requests can over-consume it.

#### Reachability

The request capacity is not bounded by validation. `validateExactDeviceRequest` (`pkg/apis/resource/validation/validation.go`) validates the device class, selectors, allocation mode, count, and tolerations, but not the `Capacity` field, so a claim may carry any positive int64 in `request.capacity.requests[name]`. The device-side policy is validated (`Min + Step <= capacity`), but that does not bound the request. The default feature configuration selects the incubating allocator, which has this behavior.

### What did you expect to happen?

A capacity request far larger than the device capacity should be rejected, and consumed capacity should never be negative.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Add this case to the shared `allocatortesting` table:

<details>
<summary>Regression test</summary>

```go
"consumable-capacity-range-policy-step-request-overflow": {
    features: Features{
        ConsumableCapacity: true,
    },
    claimsToAllocate: objects(
        claim(claim0).withRequests(deviceRequest(req0, classA, 1).withCapacityRequest(resource.NewQuantity(9223372036854775807, resource.BinarySI))),
    ),
    classes: objects(classWithAllowMultipleAllocations(classA, driverA, true)),
    slices: unwrapResourceSlices(
        sliceWithDevices(slice1, node1, pool1, driverA,
            device(device1, nil, nil).withAllowMultipleAllocations().withCapacityRequestPolicyRange(map[resourceapi.QualifiedName]resource.Quantity{capacity0: four}),
        ),
    ),
    node:          node(node1, region1),
    expectResults: []any{},
},
```

</details>

From `staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation`, run:

```console
go test ./structured/... \
  -run 'TestAllocator/consumable-capacity-range-policy-step-request-overflow' \
  -count=1 -v
```

The device has capacity 4 with a `Min=2, Step=2, Max=4` policy, and the claim requests `math.MaxInt64`. Expected: no allocation. On current master, `device-1` is allocated (the logs show `Device allocated` and a negative `consumed capacity`), because `roundUpRange` overflowed to a negative value. The case fails on the incubating and experimental variants; stable does not support ConsumableCapacity.

### Anything else we need to know?

`roundUpRange` and `violateValidRange` both convert `resource.Quantity` to int64 via `.Value()` and do plain int64 arithmetic. #140161 reworks `CapacityRequestPolicyRange` for fractional quantities but does not touch this overflow. A fix could compute the rounding with `resource.Quantity` arithmetic (or saturate at `math.MaxInt64`), and validation could additionally bound the request against the device capacity.

The reproduction is allocator-only and does not require a running cluster, DRA driver, container runtime, or cloud provider.

137707.title: [Scheduling] OpportunisticBatching: redundant synchronous RunFilterPlugins call in batchStateCompatible for low-resource pods
137707.body:
/kind bug
/sig scheduling

### What happened?

When OpportunisticBatching (KEP-5598) is enabled, `batchStateCompatible` performs a synchronous
`RunFilterPlugins` call on the `lastChosenNode` to validate whether the cached batch state is
still usable (i.e., the previously chosen node is now full).

For pods with low resource requirements that do not fill up a node, this check always passes
(not rejected), causing `batchStateCompatible` to always return `false`. This means:

1. **The synchronous `RunFilterPlugins` call is pure overhead** — it runs on the critical
   scheduling path, adds latency, and never yields a useful result for these pods.
2. **The same node is filtered twice** — once synchronously in `batchStateCompatible`, and again
   in the parallel `findNodesThatPassFilters` pipeline (since `lastChosenNode` is part of
   `allNodes`).
3. **The batch cache is flushed every cycle** — preventing any future batching even though the
   pod signatures match.

This is a common scenario in production clusters with many small pods (microservices, batch
workloads, etc.), where the batching optimization provides no benefit but introduces consistent
per-cycle overhead.

### What did you expect to happen?

The `batchStateCompatible` check should not introduce synchronous overhead on the critical
scheduling path when the optimization cannot provide any benefit (i.e., when pods don't fill
up nodes).

### Code reference

```go
// pkg/scheduler/framework/runtime/batch.go, line 218-222
status := b.handle.RunFilterPlugins(ctx, state, pod, lastChosenNode)
if !status.IsRejected() {
    b.logUnusableState(logger, cycleCount, metrics.BatchFlushNodeNotFull)
    return false
}
```

###  Proposed optimization

Option A: Cheap pre-check before RunFilterPluginsBefore calling RunFilterPlugins on lastChosenNode, perform a lightweight resource comparison

(pod's resource requests vs. node's remaining allocatable capacity). If the node clearly has
sufficient resources, skip the expensive RunFilterPlugins call entirely. This is O(1) and
avoids running all filter plugins.Caveat: This only covers resource-based filters and may miss non-resource filters (affinity,
taints, etc.), but it would eliminate the overhead for the common case.

Option B: Include lastChosenNode validation in the parallel filtering pipeline

Include lastChosenNode validation in the parallel filtering pipelineWhen batch state exists but validity is uncertain, include the lastChosenNode filter result
as metadata from the parallel findNodesThatPassFilters execution. After parallel filtering
completes, retroactively determine batch validity for the NEXT scheduling cycle. This shifts
the validation cost from a synchronous pre-check to being amortized within the existing
parallel workload.

139513.title: kube-proxy nftables: sync time grows super-linearly with Service count
139513.body:
### What happened? Our production clusters run kube-proxy in `ipvs` mode. We evaluated migrating to `nftables` mode and observed that `kube-proxy` takes a long time to complete a sync, with the `nft` process at 100% CPU for most of that time. This looks related to [#135639](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135639), which was addressed in v1.36. We are testing on v1.36.1 and still see multi-minute syncs. The two dominant costs we measure are: 1. the `ListAll` (`nft --json --terse list table ip kube-proxy`) that runs on every sync, including incremental syncs, and 1. the full sync re-emitting the entire table even when almost nothing changed. #### How we measured We created different numbers of Services/EndpointSlices in a test cluster and read kube-proxy logs at `--v=2`. A sync logs three lines: ``` I0529 17:51:15.687847 1 proxier.go:1094] "Syncing nftables rules" ipFamily="IPv4" fullSync=true I0529 17:52:18.984398 1 proxier.go:1712] "Reloading service nftables data" ipFamily="IPv4" numServices=44125 numEndpoints=44152 I0529 18:07:59.283867 1 proxier.go:1088] "SyncProxyRules complete" ipFamily="IPv4" elapsed="16m43.895505566s" ``` - ListAll time is roughly the gap between `"Syncing nftables rules"` and `"Reloading service nftables data"`. During this window `nft --json --terse list table ip kube-proxy` runs at 100% CPU. (This window also includes a small stale-chain delete transaction, which is negligible at these scales.) - Total time is the `elapsed=` value on `"SyncProxyRules complete"`. #### Test environment - Instance: `m6a.4xlarge` - kube-proxy: v1.36.1, `mode: nftables`. Default sync params: `minSyncPeriod=1s syncPeriod=30s maxSyncPeriod=1h0m0s`. - calico-node: v3.31.3 - Kernel: Linux 7.0 (Ubuntu 26.04); also reproduced on Linux 7.1-rc4 - Control plane: v1.33.7 - kubelet: v1.33.7 > We ran kube-proxy v1.36.1, despite the version skew against the v1.33.7 control plane and kubelet, to include the v1.36 nftables improvements (#135800, #136499). We believe the behavior we measured does not depend on the control plane or kubelet version: it is node-local nftables programming, driven only by the number of Services/EndpointSlices. If that assumption is wrong, please let us know and we can re-test on a version-matched cluster. Our production clusters reach ~44k Services at an almost 1:1 Service-to-endpoint ratio. That is a much larger Service count than #135639's repro (~1k–5k Services, with high endpoints-per-Service). So the cost here is driven by the number of Services/chains, not just endpoint fan-out, and it appears at Service counts well beyond what #135639 tested. No production workloads run on the test cluster. To trigger incremental syncs, a script creates and deletes 50 Services every 30 seconds. #### Results `fullSync=true` (full sync) vs `fullSync=false` (incremental). Each cell is the p50 across the collected syncs at that scale; the ListAll and Total values are taken from the same sync (the one at p50 of Total). | N (services ~ endpoints) | incremental — ListAll | incremental — Total | full — ListAll | full — Total | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 4,125 | 874 ms | 878 ms | 939 ms | 5.11 s | | 14,125 | 7.25 s | 7.49 s | 7.45 s | 58.25 s | | 24,125 | 20.44 s | 20.76 s | 21.48 s | 3m11.10s | | 34,125 | 39.61 s | 40.30 s | 47.19 s | 8m13.51s | | 44,125 | 1m9.01s | 1m10.14s | 1m3.30s | 16m43.90s | | 44,125 (empty kube-proxy table) | — | — | 284 ms | 4m46.84s | Observations: - From 4k to 44k Services (~11× the count), incremental sync grew ~80× and full sync grew ~197×. The growth is much steeper than linear in the number of Services. - Incremental sync is almost entirely `ListAll`. The actual write is small (<2s even at 44k); the rest is reading the whole table to discover existing chains/affinity sets for cleanup. - Full sync = `ListAll` + re-emitting the whole table. At 44k, ListAll is ~63s of the 16m43s; the remaining ~15.5m is the kernel reprocessing the full set of chains/rules during the commit. - A freshly created node (empty `kube-proxy` table) does a full sync in ~4m47s, which is _faster_ than the hourly full sync on a populated table (~16m43s). This suggests the kernel cost during commit scales with how much already exists in the table, not just with how much is being written. ### What did you expect to happen? Sync time grows too fast with Service count. We don't necessarily expect constant-time syncs, but the current growth means a single change at 44k Services already costs more than a minute (incremental) and the hourly full sync costs ~16 minutes. We'd like both to be substantially lower. #### Incremental sync At 44k Services, an incremental sync takes >1 minute, so any single change (Service create, deployment rollout) has a Network Programming Latency (NPL) over a minute on that node. This is too slow for our production use case. We would like incremental NPL to be on the order of seconds (e.g. p50 ~30s or better) at this scale. Incremental sync calls `ListAll` (reads existing chains and affinity sets) on every run. Could kube-proxy keep an in-memory copy of the committed state and skip `ListAll` on incremental syncs? All writes to the nftables table go through transactions, and in normal operation nothing else modifies kube-proxy's table, so trusting the in-memory copy seems safe, with a periodic full sync as the reconciliation/safety net. #### Full sync Full sync runs at kube-proxy startup and every hour. At 44k, a full sync takes ~16m. During that window the data plane keeps working on the previously committed rules, but any Service/EndpointSlice change that arrives during the full sync is not reflected on the node until the full sync finishes. NPL can spike to ~16m once per hour. We would like the hourly full sync to be ~1m at p50 at this scale. The first full sync at startup taking longer is acceptable. Today full sync writes all Service/EndpointSlice data from the informer to nftables regardless of whether it already matches the kernel. Could full sync use its `ListAll` result to diff actual vs desired state and write only the differences? ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? We use [https://github.com/haojiwu/k8s-scale-test](https://github.com/haojiwu/k8s-scale-test) to create synthetic Services + EndpointSlices: ``` # Create ~44k Services, each with 1 synthetic endpoint. # (apiserver-bound; takes a while to create all objects.) KUBE_CONTEXT= ./k8s-scale-test.sh load 44125 # Continuously create/delete Services to trigger incremental syncs. KUBE_CONTEXT= ./k8s-scale-test.sh churn ``` Then restart the kube-proxy pod and read the new pod's logs: - the first sync after pod creation is a full sync (`fullSync=true`) - subsequent syncs driven by churn are incremental (`fullSync=false`) We also reproduced on a Linux 7.1-rc4 kernel; results are similar. ### Anything else we need to know? _No response_ ### Kubernetes version
